noteRef.topicTitle: The nature and variety of living organisms

specPoints.text: understand how living organisms share the following characteristics: • they require nutrition • they respire • they excrete their waste • they respond to their surroundings • they move • they control their internal conditions • they reproduce • they grow and develop.

primer.text: Before anything else can be studied, biology needs its definition of life. Every living organism, from bacteria to sunflowers to you, carries out the same eight processes — movement, then respiration, then sensitivity, then control, then growth, then reproduction, then excretion and finally nutrition. This note walks each process in turn, contrasts the plant and animal versions, and fixes the exam's favourite distinctions, including excretion versus egestion.

lessons.title: The life processes: nutrition, respiration and excretion
lessons.opening: Life has a checklist. The note opens with the eight unifying characteristics — movement, then respiration, then sensitivity, then control, then growth, then reproduction, then excretion and finally nutrition — then takes the first three in detail. Organisms obtain food for energy and growth, release that energy through respiration, and eliminate the toxic wastes their cell chemistry produces.
keyPoints: Every living organism carries out the same eight life processes, remembered as MRS C GREN.
Organisms need nutrition for energy and growth materials: plants photosynthesise, animals consume and digest.
Respiration is a chemical process in all living organisms that releases energy from glucose, aerobically or anaerobically.
Excretion removes toxic waste from chemical reactions in cells: carbon dioxide, water and urea in animals; oxygen and carbon dioxide in plants.
Excretion must not be confused with egestion — faeces come from unabsorbed food, not cell reactions.

low.restatement: Living things all do the same eight jobs: take in food, release energy from it, and get rid of the poisonous leftovers.
low.analogy: Think of MRS C GREN as the entry checklist at a hotel for life — miss one item and the particle does not get to check in as living.
low.examPointer: Exam questions name a process and ask for its definition or its plant and animal versions — learn all three columns for each process.

medium.restatement: The eight characteristics apply universally: nutrition feeds respiration, respiration powers everything, and excretion clears the toxic products of the chemistry that respiration and other reactions generate.
medium.analogy: A car burns fuel and moves, but it never grows, reproduces or excretes the products of its own cell chemistry — that is why it fails the life checklist.
medium.examPointer: The classic trap is excretion versus egestion: anchor excretion to waste made by chemical reactions in cells and egestion to faeces from unabsorbed food.

check.stem: Which set completes the acronym MRS C GREN, the checklist of the eight processes every living organism carries out?

options.text: Movement, then respiration, then sensitivity, then control, then growth, then reproduction, then excretion and finally nutrition
options.explanation: These are the eight characteristics of life the note lists in order.

options.text: Movement, respiration, sensitivity, consumption, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition
options.explanation: The C stands for control (homeostasis), not consumption.

options.text: Movement, respiration, sensitivity, control, germination, reproduction, excretion, nutrition
options.explanation: Germination is a stage in plant growth, not one of the eight processes.

options.text: Motion, respiration, sensitivity, control, growth, recycling, excretion, nutrition
options.explanation: Motion is not the listed term and recycling is not a life process.

check.stem: A student observes a particle that reproduces inside host cells but never respires, excretes or grows. How should it be classified?

options.text: Non-living, because reproduction alone does not satisfy every characteristic of life
options.explanation: Something is living only if it carries out all eight processes; viruses are the note's example.

options.text: Living, because reproduction is the process that defines life
options.explanation: Reproduction is one necessary process among eight, not a sufficient one.

options.text: Living, because it responds to its host cells
options.explanation: Hijacking a host cell is not sensitivity in the characteristic-of-life sense.

options.text: Dead, because it cannot move on its own
options.explanation: Dead implies it was once a complete living organism; a virus never satisfies the full checklist.

check.stem: Which list gives the waste products that animals excrete?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, water and urea
options.explanation: These are the three animal excretory products the note lists, from respiration and protein breakdown.

options.text: Oxygen, water and urea
options.explanation: Oxygen is a plant waste product from photosynthesis, not an animal one.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, glucose and urea
options.explanation: Glucose is the respiratory substrate, not a waste product.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, water and faeces
options.explanation: Faeces are egested, not excreted — they never come from cell chemical reactions.

check.stem: Which pairing of organism and excretory waste is correct?

options.text: Plants excrete oxygen from photosynthesis during daylight
options.explanation: The note lists oxygen from photosynthesis and carbon dioxide from respiration as plant wastes.

options.text: Plants excrete urea from protein breakdown
options.explanation: Urea is the animal waste from deaminating proteins; plants do not make it.

options.text: Animals excrete oxygen from respiration
options.explanation: Respiration consumes oxygen; animals excrete carbon dioxide from it.

options.text: Plants excrete carbon dioxide only at night
options.explanation: Respiration runs day and night; the net gas seen by day is oxygen from photosynthesis.

check.stem: Which statement about respiration is true for every living organism?

options.text: It is a chemical process that releases energy from glucose
options.explanation: Respiration runs in all living cells, releasing energy from glucose via ATP.

options.text: It is the same process as gas exchange
options.explanation: Gas exchange moves the gases; respiration uses the oxygen to release energy — the note's own hint.

options.text: It happens only in animals with lungs
options.explanation: All living organisms respire, plant and microbe included.

options.text: It builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water
options.explanation: That is photosynthesis; respiration breaks glucose down.

check.stem: State the word equation for aerobic respiration.
check.modelAnswer: Glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water (with energy transferred as ATP).

check.stem: Name the nutrition route of plants and the nutrition route of animals, as the note contrasts them.
check.modelAnswer: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis; animals consume other organisms and break food down by digestion.

check.stem: Students often mix up excretion and egestion. Explain the difference the note draws, in terms of where the waste comes from.
check.modelAnswer: Excretion removes toxic waste made by chemical reactions inside cells, such as carbon dioxide and urea; egestion passes out faeces, which are the remains of food never absorbed during digestion.

check.stem: A pond appears to contain only inert gravel, yet the water carries single-celled organisms. Which processes would you look for to decide they are living, and what conclusion follows if even one process is absent?
check.modelAnswer: Look for all eight MRS C GREN processes — nutrition, respiration, excretion, sensitivity, movement, control, growth and reproduction; if any one is absent the particle is non-living rather than living.

lessons.title: Sensitivity, control, reproduction and growth
lessons.opening: The second half of the checklist covers how organisms sense and respond, move, hold their insides steady, make more of themselves and grow. Animals answer their surroundings with electrical impulses and hormones, plants answer slowly with tropisms, and every lineage reproduces — sexually with fused gametes or asexually as a clone.
keyPoints: Sensitivity is detecting and responding to stimuli: electrical impulses via the nervous system, hormones via the endocrine system.
Plants respond chemically and slowly: geotropism towards gravity, phototropism towards light.
Movement is a change of position or place; plants change orientation instead of moving from place to place.
Homeostasis keeps internal conditions within required limits — thermoregulation near 37 degrees Celsius and osmoregulation of water levels.
Sexual reproduction fuses gametes so offspring carry DNA from both parents; asexual reproduction needs one parent and produces a clone.

low.restatement: Organisms sense their surroundings, move, hold their insides steady, reproduce and grow — the second half of the life checklist.
low.analogy: If MRS C GREN is the checklist, this lesson is the back page: sense it, move it, keep it steady, copy it, grow it.
low.examPointer: Learn the paired examples — phototropism with light, geotropism with gravity, thermoregulation with 37 degrees — the exam asks for the pair, not the word alone.

medium.restatement: Response, movement, control and reproduction interlock: tropisms are both sensitivity and growth in direction, transpiration is control through evaporation, and reproduction secures the species.
medium.analogy: A thermostat holds a house near its set point the way thermoregulation holds a body near 37 degrees — both are control systems with a target.
medium.examPointer: Do not let phototropism and geotropism swap partners in the answer line — light belongs to the shoot, gravity to the root.

check.stem: Which signalling method does the human nervous system use to respond to stimuli?

options.text: Electrical impulses travelling through receptors, neurones and effectors
options.explanation: The note describes the nervous system's electrical signalling via receptors, neurones and effectors.

options.text: Hormones carried in the blood
options.explanation: Hormones are the endocrine system's chemical messengers, not the nervous system's.

options.text: Diffusion of chemicals through the air
options.explanation: Responses are signalled inside the body, not by air diffusion.

options.text: Muscle contraction only
options.explanation: Muscles are effectors; the signalling method is electrical impulses.

check.stem: A shoot grows towards the light while a root grows down into the soil. Which pair of responses names this?

options.text: Phototropism in the shoot and geotropism in the root
options.explanation: Phototropism is the response to light; geotropism is the response to gravity.

options.text: Geotropism in the shoot and phototropism in the root
options.explanation: The two responses are swapped.

options.text: Phototropism in both, because both track a stimulus
options.explanation: The root's trigger is gravity, not light.

options.text: Geotropism in both, because both respond to the earth
options.explanation: The shoot's trigger is light.

check.stem: Which processes make up the plant's asexual reproduction routes named in the note?

options.text: Natural runners and artificial cuttings
options.explanation: The note lists runners as the natural route and cuttings as the artificial one.

options.text: Pollination and fertilisation
options.explanation: Those belong to sexual reproduction in plants.

options.text: Mitosis and meiosis
options.explanation: Mitosis is the cell process behind asexual reproduction; meiosis makes gametes for sexual reproduction.

options.text: Germination and dispersal
options.explanation: Those are growth and spreading stages, not asexual reproduction routes.

check.stem: Why is transpiration counted among a plant's control (homeostasis) mechanisms?

options.text: Evaporating water from the stomata carries heat out, holding the leaf near its optimum
options.explanation: The note's control section credits transpiration's evaporation with maintaining a suitable temperature.

options.text: Transpiration pulls minerals up from the roots
options.explanation: That is the transport role of transpiration, not temperature control.

options.text: Transpiration closes the stomata at night
options.explanation: Stomatal closing is a separate response; the control benefit is evaporative heat loss.

options.text: Transpiration produces glucose for growth
options.explanation: Glucose comes from photosynthesis.

check.stem: Which statement about sexual reproduction is correct?

options.text: Gametes fuse, so the offspring carries DNA from both parents
options.explanation: The note: male and female gametes fuse and the offspring's DNA combines maternal and paternal DNA.

options.text: One parent produces an exact clone
options.explanation: That describes asexual reproduction.

options.text: The offspring's DNA is identical to the parent's
options.explanation: Fusion of two gametes mixes DNA.

options.text: Gametes are made by mitosis in animals
options.explanation: The note names sperm and egg as the gametes without mitosis claims; mitosis is the asexual example.

check.stem: Define homeostasis as the note introduces it.
check.modelAnswer: Homeostasis is the control of an organism's internal environment to keep conditions within required limits.

check.stem: State the optimum human body temperature and the two cooling mechanisms the note lists for returning to it.
check.modelAnswer: 37 degrees Celsius; sweating and vasodilation bring a raised temperature back down.

check.stem: Explain why osmoregulation is described as another homeostatic mechanism in humans, alongside thermoregulation.
check.modelAnswer: Both hold an internal condition within required limits — thermoregulation holds body temperature near 37 degrees Celsius, while osmoregulation controls water levels; each is a control process keeping the internal environment stable.

check.stem: A sunflower changes its orientation to track the sun through the day. Identify the two life processes this shows and justify each from the note's definitions.
check.modelAnswer: Movement — the plant changes its orientation, the note's stated plant form of movement; and sensitivity — tracking the sun is a response to a stimulus in the surroundings.

glossary.definition: The acronym for the eight life processes: movement, respiration, sensitivity, control, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition.
The control of an organism's internal environment to keep conditions within required limits, such as thermoregulation and osmoregulation.
A sex cell — sperm in human males, eggs in human females, pollen nuclei and ovules in plants — that fuses with another in sexual reproduction.
A plant's response to light, which causes shoots to grow towards the sunlight.

Plants maintain an optimum temperature through transpiration
Sexual reproduction involves the fusing of two gametes to form a zygote that contains DNA from both parents

figures.caption: Asexual reproduction in bacteria involves creating exact copies of the parent cell
